# Change-of-Control Extraction Report

## Executive Summary

This report reviews 8 acquisition-target contracts for change-of-control provisions. Each contract is analyzed below in a dedicated section that surfaces the change-of-control / anti-assignment definition, consent and termination triggers, financial exposures, reverse-triangular-merger analysis, and risk rating. The structured data behind these analyses (a 28-column extraction) is appended as a reference table.

## Per-Contract Findings

### hesse-employment-agreement

**Employment Agreement — Dr. Miriam Hesse (CTO) | Governing Law: Ohio**

This is an at-will employment agreement (Agreement No. EA-2021-003-MH, effective August 15, 2021) between Apex Industrial Technologies, Inc. and Dr. Miriam Hesse, serving as Chief Technology Officer, governed by the laws of the State of Ohio pursuant to Section 8.4. The agreement carries a HIGH risk rating, driven by a single-trigger equity acceleration provision, an unresolved conflict with the Merger Agreement's RSU rollover mechanism, and Executive's consent status as a potential closing condition.

**Change of Control Definition — Section 1**

Section 1 provides a four-prong definition of "Change of Control": (i) any merger, consolidation, reorganization, or similar business combination in which the Company is not the surviving entity or in which pre-transaction shareholders hold less than fifty percent (50%) of the surviving entity's voting securities; (ii) sale, transfer, or other disposition of all or substantially all assets; (iii) acquisition by any person or group of beneficial ownership of more than fifty percent (50%) of combined voting power; or (iv) replacement of a majority of the Board within any twenty-four (24) consecutive months. The structured findings confirm that indirect ownership changes are not captured (coc_includes_indirect: False), meaning only direct Company-level events trigger the definition. Critically, the pending reverse-triangular merger — in which Voltan Acquisition Sub, Inc. merges into Apex with Apex surviving as a wholly-owned subsidiary of Voltan Manufacturing Group, Inc. — satisfies the second prong of trigger (i): although the Company is the surviving legal entity, pre-merger Apex shareholders will hold zero percent of the surviving entity post-close. The Exhibit A Side Letter expressly confirms this reading: "the consummation of the Merger constitutes a 'Change of Control' as defined in Section 1 of the Employment Agreement."

**Single-Trigger Equity Acceleration — Section 5.4**

Section 5.4 states: "upon the consummation of a Change of Control, all of Executive's then-unvested Equity Awards shall immediately and automatically vest and, to the extent applicable, become exercisable in full" and that this "shall occur automatically upon the consummation of a Change of Control and shall not require any termination of Executive's employment or any other condition or contingency." Section 6.6 further confirms: "the equity acceleration provided under Section 5.4 is not conditioned upon the execution of a release of claims and shall operate automatically." As of the Side Letter date, Executive holds 45,000 unvested RSUs under the Apex Industrial Technologies, Inc. 2021 Equity Incentive Plan. At the Exchange Ratio of 0.3142 and a 30-day VWAP of $68.42 per Parent share (implying a per-Company-share value of $21.494), automatic acceleration yields an aggregate value of approximately $967,230 — a direct cash-equivalent exposure to the acquirer on Day 1 of closing. Section 5.4 expressly supersedes any contrary provision in individual award agreements or the 2021 Equity Incentive Plan.

**Conflict Between Section 5.4 and Merger Agreement Section 3.05**

Section 3.05 of the Merger Agreement contemplates RSU Rollover Treatment: unvested Company RSUs convert into unvested Parent RSUs on the same vesting schedule, covering approximately 14,139 Parent RSUs. Section 5.4 of the Employment Agreement would cause all 45,000 Company RSUs to vest immediately at closing — directly negating the rollover. The Side Letter (Section 1) explicitly acknowledges this conflict: "these provisions are in direct conflict and that, absent a resolution of such conflict, the consummation of the Merger would trigger the single-trigger acceleration of Executive's unvested Equity Awards under Section 5.4 of the Employment Agreement, notwithstanding the RSU Rollover Treatment contemplated by the Merger Agreement." Critically, Side Letter Section 3 confirms that "Section 5.4 of the Employment Agreement remains in full force and effect and has not been amended or waived by this Side Letter" — meaning the $967,230 acceleration exposure is live and unresolved as of the date of this review.

**Consent Requirements and Closing Condition Risk — Section 4 (Side Letter) / Merger Agreement Section 7.03(c)**

Side Letter Section 4 acknowledges that "Executive's consent to the RSU Rollover Treatment, or a waiver by Executive of the single-trigger acceleration right under Section 5.4 of the Employment Agreement, may constitute a Required Consent under Section 7.03(c) of the Merger Agreement," which requires Required Consents to be obtained at least five (5) business days prior to the Closing Date. Absent Executive's agreement, Section 5.4 remains operative and the rollover cannot proceed as structured — giving Dr. Hesse meaningful leverage over the deal timeline ahead of the expected August 29, 2025 closing.

**Anti-Assignment — Section 8.3**

Section 8.3 permits Company assignment "to any successor in interest to all or substantially all of the Company's business or assets, whether by merger, consolidation, sale of assets, or otherwise, provided that any such successor expressly assumes and agrees to perform the Company's obligations under this Agreement." Because Apex survives the reverse-triangular merger, there is no automatic assignment to Parent — but the express assumption requirement must be confirmed in the Merger Agreement (specifically Section 3.05) to prevent Executive from asserting a Good Reason resignation based on a material breach by the Company under the Good Reason definition in Section 1.

**Double-Trigger Severance Exposure — Section 5.3**

Even if the single-trigger acceleration issue is resolved pre-closing, Section 5.3 creates a contingent double-trigger exposure: if Executive is terminated without Cause or resigns for Good Reason within twenty-four (24) months following closing, she is entitled to a lump-sum severance of $1,232,000 (calculated as ($385,000 Base Salary + $231,000 Target Bonus) × 2.0x), plus 24 months of COBRA continuation and pro-rata bonus. Section 5.5 imposes a Section 280G/4999 cutback mechanism — the $967,230 RSU acceleration value must be included in the parachute payment calculation immediately.

**Risk Rating: HIGH**

The rating is driven by: (1) unwaived single-trigger acceleration of $967,230 in RSU value that fires automatically at closing absent a negotiated resolution; (2) Executive's consent constituting a potential closing condition under Merger Agreement Section 7.03(c), creating deal-blocking leverage; and (3) a contingent $1,232,000 double-trigger severance tail within the 24-month post-closing window.

**Action Items:**
1. Negotiate and execute Executive's waiver of single-trigger acceleration under Section 5.4 in exchange for mutually agreed consideration before the Closing Date (expected August 29, 2025), consistent with Side Letter Section 3; ensure the waiver instrument satisfies Section 8.2 (written, signed by both parties).
2. Confirm Executive's consent to RSU Rollover Treatment constitutes a Required Consent under Merger Agreement Section 7.03(c) and obtain such consent at least 5 business days prior to closing.
3. Confirm that Section 3.05 of the Merger Agreement (or a separate assumption agreement) expressly assumes Company obligations under the Employment Agreement, as required by Section 8.3, to foreclose any Good Reason claim by Executive post-closing.
4. Include the $967,230 RSU acceleration value in the Section 280G/4999 parachute payment analysis under Section 5.5 before closing.
5. Coordinate retention terms with Dr. Hesse to manage the $1,232,000 double-trigger severance exposure under Section 5.3 within the 24-month post-closing window.

### apex-kenji-jv-agreement

**Apex-Kenji Precision JV, LLC — Joint Venture Agreement (apex-kenji-jv-agreement)**

This is a Joint Venture Agreement governing Apex-Kenji Precision JV, LLC, a Delaware limited liability company, between Apex Industrial Technologies, Inc. (55% member) and counterparty Kenji Valve Co., Ltd. (45% member). The agreement is governed by Delaware law per Section 17.2.

**Change-of-Control Definition — Article I**

The agreement contains an express and broadly drafted Change-of-Control definition in Article I: "'Change of Control' means, with respect to any Member, the acquisition, directly or indirectly, by any Person or group of Persons acting in concert (other than such Member's existing Affiliates as of the Effective Date), of fifty percent (50%) or more of the issued and outstanding voting equity interests of such Member, whether by purchase, merger, consolidation, recapitalization, reorganization, or otherwise, or any transaction or series of related transactions that results in a change in the power to direct or cause the direction of the management and policies of such Member." The definition expressly captures indirect acquisitions and alternative structural forms, including mergers and consolidations. Critically, the Article I definition of "Transfer" further reinforces this scope: Transfer encompasses "any direct or indirect sale, assignment, pledge, encumbrance, hypothecation, gift, or other disposition of all or any portion of a Membership Interest, whether voluntary or involuntary, by operation of law or otherwise." This means even involuntary or law-operation transfers are captured. A reverse-triangular merger in which Apex survives as a wholly-owned subsidiary of an Acquirer would satisfy the 50% threshold — the Acquirer acquires 100% of Apex's voting equity, unambiguously triggering the definition.

**Anti-Assignment / Transfer Restriction — Section 11.1**

Section 11.1 imposes a general transfer prohibition: "No Member shall Transfer all or any portion of its Membership Interest without the prior written consent of the other Member, which consent may be withheld in such Member's sole and absolute discretion, except as expressly provided in Sections 11.2 and 11.3 of this Agreement." Notably, however, Section 12.2 expressly carves out a Change of Control from Section 11.1's consent requirement: "a Change of Control of a Member shall not be deemed a Transfer of such Member's Membership Interest for purposes of Article XI. Accordingly, a Change of Control shall not require the consent of the non-affected Member under Section 11.1." Accordingly, no separate consent right arises — but the carve-out is not cost-free; it feeds directly into Section 12.3's buy-out mechanism.

**Buy-Out Option — Section 12.3: The Core Financial Consequence Chain**

Upon a Change of Control of Apex, Kenji (the Non-Affected Member) receives an automatic buy-out right under Section 12.3(a): the right "to purchase all (but not less than all) of the Affected Member's Membership Interest." Kenji may exercise this option "by delivering written notice to the Affected Member within ninety (90) days following receipt of the notice of consummation of the Change of Control." If exercised, closing must occur within sixty (60) days of the exercise notice per Section 12.3(d).

The Buy-Out Price under Section 12.3(c) is "equal to four and one-half times (4.5x) the Company's trailing twelve-month EBITDA as of the last day of the Company's most recently completed Fiscal Year preceding the date of the Non-Affected Member's exercise notice." With FY2024 EBITDA of $5,100,000, the current Buy-Out Price equals approximately **$22.95 million** — representing the forced divestiture of Apex's entire 55% JV interest regardless of percentage held, payable "in cash at closing" by wire transfer per Section 12.3(d)(ii). This exposure is in addition to the $14.8 million in annual JV revenue attributable to Apex (representing approximately 7.9% of Apex's TTM revenue of ~$187.4 million) that would be at risk upon JV unwind. EBITDA calculation disputes are resolved under Section 12.3(e) by a mutually agreed independent nationally recognized accounting firm (or AAA-selected if no agreement within 15 days), with costs split equally.

**Successor Entity Carve-Out — Section 12.3(b): Two-Condition Analysis**

The Buy-Out Option is extinguished only if BOTH of the following conditions are satisfied simultaneously:

*Condition (i):* "the Successor Entity commits, in writing delivered to the Non-Affected Member within thirty (30) days following consummation of the Change of Control, to maintain the Affected Member's existing senior management team (including, at a minimum, the Affected Member's chief executive officer and chief technology officer) in their respective positions for a period of not less than eighteen (18) months following the consummation of the Change of Control."

*Condition (ii):* "the Successor Entity's consolidated annual revenue derived from fluid control products (including, without limitation, valves, actuators, flow meters, and related automation systems), as reported in the Successor Entity's most recent audited annual financial statements as of the date of consummation of the Change of Control, exceeds Five Hundred Million Dollars ($500,000,000)."

The agreement is explicit: "Both conditions (i) and (ii) above must be satisfied for this Section 12.3(b) carve-out to apply. If either condition is not met, the Buy-Out Option shall remain fully exercisable by the Non-Affected Member in accordance with Section 12.3(a)." The source text's Recitals flag the competitive context directly, noting that Voltan Manufacturing Group's flow control division generates approximately $410,000,000 in consolidated annual revenue — below the $500 million threshold. Any Acquirer with a similar or smaller fluid control revenue profile would fail Condition (ii), leaving the Buy-Out Option fully live.

**Notice Obligations — Section 12.1**

Apex faces a dual notice obligation: (1) written notice to Kenji "within ten (10) business days" after execution of any definitive merger agreement, and (2) a second notice "within five (5) business days following the consummation" of the Change of Control. Both notices must include the identity of the acquiring Person and expected/actual consummation date. These notice obligations are mechanical and time-sensitive; failure to comply would leave the 90-day buy-out exercise window ambiguous.

**Joinder and Continuing Obligations — Section 12.4**

Regardless of whether Kenji exercises the Buy-Out Option, Section 12.4(b) requires the Successor Entity to "execute a joinder agreement in form and substance reasonably satisfactory to the Non-Affected Member" within thirty (30) days post-closing. Section 12.4(a) further preserves all Affected Member obligations, binding the Successor Entity to the full Agreement.

**Cross-Referenced Contracts**

The Technology License Agreement between Apex and the Company and the Distribution Access Agreement between Kenji and the Company (both executed concurrently, per Exhibit B) are not part of this contract's scope but are critically relevant: each may contain independent CoC or consent-to-assignment provisions that would separately trigger on the merger. These must be reviewed as standalone items.

**Risk Rating: HIGH**

The risk rating is HIGH. A Change of Control of Apex automatically triggers Kenji's buy-out right under Section 12.3(a) at 4.5x trailing EBITDA — approximately $22.95 million in cash, representing forced divestiture of Apex's 55% JV interest. The Section 12.3(b) carve-out requires Acquirer to satisfy both a $500 million fluid control revenue threshold AND an 18-month written CEO/CTO retention commitment within 30 days post-closing — conditions that are deal-specific and cannot be assumed satisfied. JV revenue of $14.8 million (~7.9% of Apex TTM revenue) is at risk if the JV unwinds.

**Action Items:**
1. Confirm whether Acquirer's consolidated annual fluid control revenue exceeds $500,000,000 per Section 12.3(b)(ii) prior to signing.
2. Confirm whether Acquirer can deliver a written 18-month retention commitment for Apex's CEO and CTO within 30 days post-closing per Section 12.3(b)(i).
3. Deliver first written CoC notice to Kenji within 10 business days of signing the definitive merger agreement per Section 12.1.
4. Deliver second written CoC notice to Kenji within 5 business days of closing per Section 12.1.
5. Prepare financing or reserves for potential $22.95 million cash buy-out demand exercisable within 90 days post-closing per Section 12.3(a).
6. Ensure Successor Entity executes joinder agreement satisfactory to Kenji within 30 days post-closing per Section 12.4(b).
7. Engage an independent accounting firm pre-closing to align on EBITDA calculation methodology and prevent Buy-Out Price disputes under Section 12.3(e).
8. Review the Technology License Agreement and Distribution Access Agreement referenced in Exhibit B for independent CoC or consent-to-assignment provisions that may separately trigger on the merger.

### hendricks-license-agreement

**Hendricks Automation Systems, Inc. — Technology License Agreement (No. HAS-LIC-2020-0088) | License | Massachusetts Law**

This is a Technology License Agreement dated March 1, 2020, between Hendricks Automation Systems, Inc. (Licensor, "Hendricks") and Apex Industrial Technologies, Inc. (Licensee, "Apex"), governed by the laws of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts. The agreement licenses Hendricks's proprietary FlowLogic Predictive Maintenance Algorithm — embedded as a core component of Apex's AX-7000 Product Line — on a non-exclusive, non-transferable, royalty-bearing basis through February 28, 2030.

**Change-of-Control Definition (Section 1.3)**

Section 1.3 defines "Change of Control" with exceptional breadth, capturing: "(a) any merger, consolidation, or reorganization involving Licensee, whether or not Licensee is the surviving entity; (b) the sale, transfer, or other disposition of all or substantially all of Licensee's assets; (c) the acquisition by any person or group of persons of beneficial ownership of more than fifty percent (50%) of the outstanding voting securities of Licensee; or (d) any other transaction or series of related transactions that results in a change in the identity of the person or persons who ultimately control Licensee." Critically, the definition adds: "a Change of Control shall be deemed to have occurred regardless of the form of transaction, including without limitation forward mergers, reverse mergers, triangular mergers, and any combination thereof." No structured finding or source text supplies a separate indirect-ownership CoC threshold, and the Section 1.3 definition is Licensee-side only — Licensor's own change of control is not a triggering event.

**Reverse-Triangular Merger Analysis**

The explicit enumeration of "reverse mergers, triangular mergers, and any combination thereof" in Section 1.3 eliminates any structural argument that a reverse-triangular merger — in which Apex survives as a wholly-owned subsidiary of the acquirer — avoids triggering the clause. This language was plainly drafted to foreclose that defense, and it succeeds.

**Anti-Assignment and Consent (Section 10.1)**

Section 10.1 provides that "Licensee shall not assign, transfer, delegate, or otherwise dispose of this Agreement or any of its rights or obligations hereunder, whether by operation of law or otherwise, without the prior written consent of Licensor, which consent may be withheld in Licensor's sole and absolute discretion." The clause further specifies that "a Change of Control of Licensee shall be deemed an assignment by operation of law," closing the gap that sometimes permits survivorship arguments in merger structures. Unauthorized assignment is "null and void and of no force or effect." The consent standard — "sole and absolute discretion" — is the most permissive standard available to Licensor and affords Apex no contractual leverage to compel consent.

**Immediate Termination Right (Section 9.1)**

Section 9.1 grants Licensor the right to "terminate this Agreement immediately upon written notice to Licensee in the event that Licensee undergoes a Change of Control." The clause is unambiguous: "The right of termination under this Section 9.1 shall be exercisable at Licensor's sole and absolute discretion, without obligation to justify such decision, and shall not require any prior notice period, cure period, or opportunity for Licensee to obtain Licensor's consent to the applicable Change of Control transaction. Upon delivery of Licensor's written notice of termination under this Section 9.1, termination shall be effective immediately." This contrasts sharply with the Section 9.2 material-breach termination right, which requires sixty (60) days' written notice and a cure period — underscoring that the CoC termination right was deliberately stripped of any cushion.

**Post-Termination Sell-Off Period (Section 9.5(c))**

Section 9.5(c) provides the only partial buffer: Apex may sell "existing inventory of Licensed Products that were fully manufactured prior to the effective date of termination" during a ninety (90) day Sell-Off Period, subject to continued royalty obligations. No new Licensed Products may be manufactured during this period. Given that the FlowLogic Algorithm is embedded at the hardware/firmware level in the AX-7000 (per Exhibit A's Integration Layer description), AX-7000 units not fully assembled pre-termination cannot be completed and sold.

**IP Ownership Chain — Sections 2.4 and 5.2**

Sections 2.4 and 5.2 compound the risk profile. Section 5.2 provides that "[a]ny improvements, modifications, enhancements, or Derivative Works of the Licensed Technology developed by Licensee, whether with or without Licensor's consent, shall be owned exclusively by Licensor." Combined with Section 2.4's assignment of Derivative Works to Licensor, any FlowLogic enhancements Apex has developed over the four-year life of this agreement will remain with Hendricks upon termination — potentially stripping Apex of proprietary improvements it has made to its own product's predictive maintenance functionality.

**Financial Exposure**

The structured findings quantify revenue exposure at $52,000,000 — representing AX-7000 Product Line revenue dependent on continued FlowLogic licensure. Revenue concentration percentage was not extracted and should be confirmed with Apex's finance team. At a 3.5% royalty rate (Section 4.2 and Exhibit B), annualized royalty outflow on $52M of Net Sales Revenue would be approximately $1.82M per year, illustrating the financial relationship between the parties. No termination fee or buyout formula exists — upon a Section 9.1 termination, Apex's only monetary obligation is payment of accrued royalties (Section 9.5(d)) and compliance with the Section 9.5(b) technology-return/destruction obligation.

**Crestline ERP Dependency**

The Recitals and Section 3.2 confirm that the FlowLogic Algorithm has been "configured and optimized to operate within the Crestline ERP Platform v.8.2 data architecture" and that Exhibit A's Data Ingestion Module is designed specifically for "compatibility with the Crestline ERP Platform v.8.2 data exchange APIs." This deep technical integration means termination of this agreement would not be operationally clean — it would require unwinding FlowLogic from Apex's ERP production-scheduling, quality-control, and maintenance-telemetry data flows simultaneously.

**Risk Rating: CRITICAL**

The risk rating is CRITICAL. Section 9.1 grants Licensor an immediate, no-notice, no-cure termination right upon any Change of Control, exercisable at sole and absolute discretion. Section 1.3 explicitly captures reverse-triangular mergers by name, eliminating structural protections. Section 10.1 prohibits assignment (including by operation of law) without consent Hendricks may withhold for any reason. The FlowLogic Algorithm is a core embedded component of Apex's primary product line, and termination would eliminate Apex's ability to manufacture or sell AX-7000 units — exposing $52,000,000 in revenue with zero cure period and no contractual path to compel consent.

**Action Items**

1. Obtain Hendricks's written consent to the Change of Control transaction under Section 10.1 prior to closing — this is a mandatory pre-closing condition given Licensor's unrestricted right to withhold consent.
2. Negotiate a binding waiver or amendment of Section 9.1's immediate termination right, or a standstill agreement prohibiting Hendricks from exercising it post-closing.
3. Confirm AX-7000 revenue concentration as a percentage of Apex's TTM total revenue to properly size this exposure for deal committee.
4. Confirm with IP counsel whether any Apex-developed FlowLogic enhancements have vested in Hendricks under Sections 2.4 and 5.2, and assess the scope of that IP loss in the acquisition context.
5. Separately assess the Crestline ERP Platform v.8.2 agreement for independent CoC triggers, given the deep FlowLogic–Crestline integration dependency.
6. Evaluate feasibility of sourcing a replacement predictive-maintenance algorithm for the AX-7000 as contingency against a Section 9.1 termination exercise.
7. Assess the Section 9.5(c) 90-day Sell-Off Period against Apex's current AX-7000 finished-goods and WIP inventory levels to quantify operational runway in a termination scenario.

### credit-agreement-summit

**Credit Agreement — Summit National Bank, N.A. (Administrative Agent) / Ridgeline Commercial Credit Corp. (Co-Lender) | Governing Law: Ohio**

This is the senior secured revolving credit facility (the "Credit Agreement") among Apex Industrial Technologies, Inc. as Borrower, Summit National Bank, N.A. as Administrative Agent and co-Lender ($45M commitment / 60% pro rata share), and Ridgeline Commercial Credit Corp. as co-Lender ($30M commitment / 40% pro rata share), providing an aggregate $75,000,000 revolving credit facility maturing September 22, 2027. As of the Effective Date, $42,500,000 is outstanding. The agreement is governed by Ohio law.

**Change-of-Control Definition — Section 1.01 (50% Threshold)**

Section 1.01 defines "Change of Control" as the occurrence of any of the following: "(a) any 'person' or 'group' (as such terms are used in Sections 13(d) and 14(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended) shall acquire, directly or indirectly, beneficial ownership (within the meaning of Rule 13d-3 promulgated by the SEC under said Act) of more than 50% of the outstanding shares of Voting Stock of the Borrower; or (b) the Borrower shall cease to own, directly or indirectly, 100% of the Equity Interests of each of its Subsidiaries (other than Apex-Kenji Precision JV, LLC, in which the Borrower shall at all times maintain an ownership interest of not less than 51%)." The "directly or indirectly" language in clause (a) captures a reverse-triangular merger structure: even where Apex survives as the legal entity, the Acquirer's acquisition of 100% of Apex's voting stock satisfies the Section 1.01(a) threshold, triggering the definition unconditionally.

**Change-of-Control — Mandatory Prepayment Chain: Section 2.09(d)**

Section 2.09(d) provides: "Upon the occurrence of a Change of Control (as defined in Section 1.01), the Borrower shall, within thirty (30) days following such Change of Control, prepay all outstanding Revolving Loans in full, together with all accrued and unpaid interest thereon, and all Commitments shall automatically terminate." The consequence chain is direct: any acquisition → Section 1.01 Change of Control triggered → Section 2.09(d) mandatory prepayment of the full $42,500,000 outstanding principal (plus accrued interest) within 30 days → automatic termination of the entire $75,000,000 revolving credit facility. There is no cure period. Additionally, Section 5.07(c) requires the Borrower to deliver written notice to the Administrative Agent of any Change of Control "within five (5) Business Days" of becoming aware, and Section 2.09(d) itself reiterates this notice obligation. Failure to deliver timely notice would independently constitute a covenant default under Section 8.01(d).

**Separate Change-in-Control Event of Default — Section 8.01(j) (35% Threshold): Critical Threshold Conflict**

Section 8.01(j) independently defines a "Change in Control" as an Event of Default: "(x) the acquisition by any person or group of persons acting in concert of beneficial ownership of more than 35% of the outstanding Voting Stock of the Borrower, or (y) individuals who, as of the Effective Date, constituted the Board of Directors of the Borrower . . . ceasing to constitute a majority of the Board of Directors of the Borrower." This section uses a 35% ownership threshold — materially lower than the 50% threshold in Section 1.01. Both thresholds are triggered by any acquisition of a majority stake. The structural inconsistency between these two provisions (50% in Section 1.01 vs. 35% in Section 8.01(j)) is significant: any acquisition of between 35% and 50% of Voting Stock would trigger Section 8.01(j) as an Event of Default (permitting acceleration of all Obligations under Section 8.02(a)) without triggering the Section 1.01 mandatory prepayment. For a control acquisition of 100% of Apex, both thresholds are independently and simultaneously satisfied. Upon the Section 8.01(j) Event of Default, Section 8.02(a) authorizes the Administrative Agent (upon direction of Required Lenders) to declare all Revolving Commitments terminated and all Obligations immediately due and payable — a faster and broader remedy than the 30-day prepayment window under Section 2.09(d).

**Section 6.03 Fundamental Changes Carve-Out — Conditions Analysis**

Section 6.03(c) permits a merger provided: (i) "the Borrower is the surviving entity"; (ii) "no Default or Event of Default has occurred and is continuing at the time of such transaction or would result therefrom"; and (iii) "the Borrower delivers to the Administrative Agent a certificate of a Responsible Officer certifying compliance with the foregoing conditions at least ten (10) Business Days prior to the consummation thereof." Critically, Section 6.03 contains an explicit savings clause: "For the avoidance of doubt, nothing in this Section 6.03 shall be deemed to constitute a waiver of, or otherwise limit the application of, the provisions of Section 2.09(d) or Section 8.01(j) hereof in connection with any transaction that constitutes a Change of Control (as defined in Section 1.01) or a Change in Control (as defined in Section 8.01(j))." Accordingly, satisfying the Section 6.03 conditions does not neutralize the CoC prepayment or Event of Default consequences — it is a necessary but wholly insufficient safe harbor.

**Anti-Assignment — Section 10.05 (Unanimous Lender Consent Required)**

Section 10.05 provides: "The Borrower may not assign or otherwise transfer any of its rights or obligations hereunder without the prior written consent of all Lenders." This standard is absolute — no reasonableness qualifier applies to Borrower assignments (in contrast to the reasonableness limitation applicable to Lender assignments). A merger or acquisition will typically constitute an assignment or transfer of the Borrower's obligations, requiring unanimous consent from both Summit National Bank, N.A. and Ridgeline Commercial Credit Corp.

**Amendment Veto — Section 10.02(e)**

Section 10.02(e) expressly requires "the written consent of each Lender" to "amend the definition of 'Change of Control' set forth in Section 1.01 or the definition of 'Change in Control' (as defined in Section 8.01(j)), or amend Section 2.09(d) or Section 8.01(j)." This gives each Lender an individual veto over any negotiated waiver or amendment of the CoC provisions — consent cannot be obtained by majority vote of Required Lenders (>50% of commitments). Both Summit National Bank, N.A. and Ridgeline Commercial Credit Corp. must independently agree.

**Financial Exposure**

The mandatory prepayment obligation under Section 2.09(d) is $42,500,000 in outstanding principal plus accrued interest, representing a direct cash obligation at closing. The TTM revenue of the Borrower is $187,400,000. The credit facility exposure therefore represents approximately 22.7% of TTM revenue. Automatic termination of the $75,000,000 facility eliminates the Borrower's primary liquidity source.

**Risk Rating: CRITICAL**

The risk is CRITICAL. The Section 1.01 Change of Control definition (>50% Voting Stock, directly or indirectly) and the Section 8.01(j) Change in Control Event of Default (>35% Voting Stock or board turnover) are both unconditionally triggered by any acquisition of majority control of Apex. The financial consequence chain — $42,500,000 outstanding drawn balance → mandatory prepayment within 30 days under Section 2.09(d) with automatic $75,000,000 facility termination, OR immediate acceleration under Section 8.02(a) upon Section 8.01(j) Event of Default — is unambiguous and unwaiveable without each Lender's individual written consent under Section 10.02(e). There is no cure period. The 50%/35% threshold inconsistency between Sections 1.01 and 8.01(j) creates additional exposure for partial acquisitions. The Section 6.03 carve-out is expressly disclaimed as a waiver.

**Action Items**

1. Obtain prior written consent of BOTH Summit National Bank, N.A. and Ridgeline Commercial Credit Corp. to the assignment and Change of Control under Section 10.05 before closing — unanimous consent required with no reasonableness qualifier on Borrower assignments.
2. Arrange refinancing or full payoff of the $42,500,000 outstanding Revolving Loans within 30 days of closing as required under Section 2.09(d); coordinate closing mechanics accordingly.
3. Assess whether the Section 8.01(j) "Change in Control" Event of Default (35% threshold, including board turnover prong) is independently triggered by the proposed merger structure and transaction documents, as acceleration under Section 8.02(a) may be demanded prior to the 30-day window under Section 2.09(d).
4. Negotiate a consent, waiver, and amendment package with both Lenders addressing Sections 1.01, 2.09(d), 8.01(j), and 10.05, noting that Section 10.02(e) requires each Lender's individual written consent to amend any of these provisions — no majority vote suffices.

### northland-refining-msa

This section addresses Contract No. MSA-2019-0042, a Master Supply Agreement between Apex Industrial Technologies, Inc. (as Supplier) and Northland Refining Corporation (as Buyer), governed by the laws of the State of Ohio (Section 15.1). The CISG is expressly excluded. The agreement is currently in its first Renewal Term, which commenced January 15, 2024 and expires January 14, 2027 (Section 13.2), with a 180-day non-renewal notice requirement.

No separate change-of-control definition exists in this contract. The entire CoC exposure runs exclusively through the anti-assignment clause in Section 14.2, which is the operative provision of concern.

Section 14.2 provides in full: "Neither Party shall assign, transfer, or delegate this Agreement or any of its rights, interests, or obligations hereunder, in whole or in part, whether by operation of law or otherwise, without the prior written consent of the other Party, which consent may be withheld in such Party's sole and absolute discretion. Any purported assignment, transfer, or delegation in violation of this Section 14.2 shall be null and void and of no force or effect." The clause thus covers (i) full and partial transfers, (ii) delegations of obligations, and (iii) transfers occurring by operation of law — the last of which is the critical phrase for merger analysis. There is no separate change-of-control trigger or termination right; the risk arises solely from treating the merger as an assignment requiring Northland's consent.

The Affiliate carve-out within Section 14.2 provides a limited exception: "either Party may assign this Agreement without the other Party's consent to an Affiliate of such Party; provided that (i) the assigning Party provides written notice to the other Party within thirty (30) days of such assignment, and (ii) the assigning Party remains jointly and severally liable for all obligations of its assignee under this Agreement." "Affiliate" is defined in Section 1.1 as any Person that "directly or indirectly controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with such Person," with "control" meaning ownership of "more than fifty percent (50%) of the voting securities or equivalent ownership interest." Whether the post-closing Apex subsidiary relationship satisfies this carve-out depends on the ultimate ownership and control structure. If Apex survives the merger as a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Acquirer, it is controlled by (not in common control with its former parent), and the carve-out — which permits an assignment by Apex to its own Affiliate — would need to be analyzed as to whether the Acquirer parent qualifies as Apex's Affiliate post-closing. This is a close question that requires deal-structure-specific legal analysis.

On the reverse-triangular merger structure: under Ohio law, which governs this agreement, and given that this is a sale-of-goods contract to which UCC § 2-210 principles apply, the explicit "by operation of law or otherwise" phrasing in Section 14.2 substantially undercuts the standard reverse-triangular merger argument that no assignment occurs because the target entity (Apex) technically survives. Ohio courts and UCC commentary treat the "operation of law" carve-in as encompassing statutory mergers, even when the contracting entity nominally survives. Accordingly, consent should be treated as required regardless of merger structure.

The consequence chain if consent is not obtained is severe. Section 14.2 expressly states that any non-consented assignment is "null and void and of no force or effect," which could expose the post-closing entity to loss of all rights under this contract. Section 2.3 establishes a Minimum Purchase Commitment of $30,000,000 per Contract Year, and Exhibit B's pricing notes confirm that "[a]nnual purchases have historically ranged between $30,000,000 and $38,000,000" — yielding a midpoint annual run-rate of approximately $34,000,000 and a remaining contract value through January 14, 2027 of up to $68,000,000 at that run rate. Loss of this supply relationship would eliminate a critical source of precision control valves, actuators, and integrated assemblies (Series AX-3000 through AX-7000) essential to Northland's refining operations, and could itself constitute a deal-breaker. Separately, under Section 4.3, if post-closing purchases fall below $25,000,000 in any Contract Year, Apex may increase unit pricing by up to 5% for the following Contract Year — a downstream pricing risk if the transition disrupts purchasing volumes.

Section 13.5 confirms that Section 14.2 expressly survives termination or expiration of the agreement, reinforcing its durability as a constraint.

No termination-specific consequence (beyond the nullity of the assignment) flows directly from Section 14.2 — there is no standalone termination right triggered by a change of control, and no termination fee or buyout formula is present.

Northland holds an absolute discretion consent right with no reasonableness constraint, the "operation of law" language reaches reverse-triangular structures under Ohio/UCC analysis, and the $30,000,000–$38,000,000 annual revenue stream at risk substantially exceeds materiality thresholds. A void assignment finding post-closing would strip Apex of its rights under this agreement with no cure path.

### pacwest-supply-agreement

This section addresses the Supply Agreement (Contract No. PWA-SUP-2021-117) between Apex Industrial Technologies, Inc. ("Apex") as supplier and PacWest Water Authority ("PacWest") as counterparty, governed by Texas law with disputes venued in Travis County (Article 15). The agreement covers a five-year initial term (June 1, 2021 through May 31, 2026), auto-renewing in one-year increments absent 180-day non-renewal notice (Sections 10.1–10.2), and carries a binding minimum annual purchase commitment of $4,000,000 per contract year (Section 2.3).

**Change of Control Definition — Section 1.1(c)**

The agreement contains a broad, four-limbed Change of Control definition at Section 1.1(c): "'Change of Control' shall mean (i) any merger, consolidation, or reorganization of Supplier with or into another entity, (ii) the sale or transfer of all or substantially all of the assets of Supplier, (iii) any transaction or series of related transactions resulting in any person or group of persons (as such terms are used in Section 13(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended) acquiring beneficial ownership of more than fifty percent (50%) of the outstanding voting securities of Supplier, or (iv) any direct or indirect change in the ultimate ownership or control of Supplier." Limb (iv) is particularly expansive: it independently captures a reverse-triangular merger in which Merger Sub merges into Apex and Apex survives as a wholly-owned subsidiary of Acquirer, because such a structure produces a "direct or indirect change in the ultimate ownership or control of Supplier" regardless of which entity is technically the surviving legal entity. Accordingly, the proposed transaction triggers Section 1.1(c) on at least two independent grounds — limb (i) (merger) and limb (iv) (indirect change of ultimate control).

**Anti-Assignment Clause — Section 12.2**

Section 12.2 provides: "Apex shall not assign this Agreement or any of its rights or obligations hereunder, whether by operation of law or otherwise, without the prior written consent of PacWest, which consent may be withheld in PacWest's sole discretion. Any attempted assignment in violation of this Section 12.2 shall be null and void and of no force or effect." The phrase "whether by operation of law or otherwise" is significant under Texas law, which applies UCC § 2-210 to sales-of-goods contracts. Because this is a goods supply agreement (precision valves, actuators, SCADA controllers), Texas courts would likely treat a statutory merger-by-operation-of-law as a triggering assignment absent this clause's carve-out. The second sentence of Section 12.2 provides a partial carve-out: a Change of Control "shall not be deemed an assignment for purposes of this Section 12.2, provided that such Change of Control is subject to the notice and consent requirements set forth in Section 10.5." This carve-out does not eliminate the consent requirement; it redirects it to Section 10.5, where the consent standard is equally absolute. The practical effect is that Section 12.2 and Section 10.5 operate in tandem rather than in conflict: a CoC is routed exclusively through Section 10.5's regime, preserving PacWest's full sole-discretion consent right.

**Consent and Termination Mechanics — Section 10.5**

Section 10.5 governs the CoC consequence chain in full. Under Section 10.5(a), "Apex shall provide written notice to PacWest of any Change of Control within ten (10) business days of the consummation thereof," including identity of the acquirer and anticipated operational impact. Upon receipt, Section 10.5(b) grants PacWest the right "in its sole discretion, to either (i) consent to the continuation of this Agreement with the successor entity or the reconstituted Supplier, as applicable, or (ii) terminate this Agreement upon ninety (90) days' written notice to Apex (or its successor)." Critically, there is no cure period: once PacWest elects termination under Section 10.5(b)(ii), the 90-day wind-down clock runs without any opportunity for Apex to remedy the change. Section 10.5(c) adds a further pressure point: "If PacWest's consent to the Change of Control is not obtained within sixty (60) days following the closing of the Change of Control transaction, PacWest may exercise its termination right under Section 10.5(b)(ii) at any time thereafter," and expressly states that PacWest's silence does not constitute consent or waiver. Section 10.5(d) requires Apex or its successor to continue fulfilling all outstanding Purchase Orders and to maintain product quality and availability throughout any notice period — a useful operational protection but not a constraint on PacWest's termination election.

**Financial Exposure**

The minimum annual purchase commitment under Section 2.3 establishes a floor exposure of $4,000,000 per contract year. Actual exposure may be materially higher depending on purchase volume tier: Exhibit C shows Tier 2 pricing applies at $6,000,000–$8,999,999 in annual volume and Tier 3 at $9,000,000 and above, suggesting PacWest's operational reliance could significantly exceed the $4M floor. The dependent systems at risk — Series PW-200, PW-400, PW-600 precision valves, Series ACT-100 actuators, and Series AXC-50 SCADA-compatible controllers — are embedded in PacWest's water treatment and distribution infrastructure and carry NSF/ANSI 61, NSF/ANSI 372, and ISO 9001:2015 certification requirements that would complicate rapid substitution of an alternative supplier, amplifying the operational consequence of a PacWest termination beyond the contractual dollar floor. No termination fee or buyout formula exists; the sole remedy for PacWest's termination under Section 10.5 is the 90-day notice period and the obligation under Section 10.5(d) to fulfill outstanding Purchase Orders during that window.

**Risk Rating: HIGH**

The rating is HIGH. PacWest holds an absolute-discretion termination right on 90 days' notice with no cure period (Section 10.5(b)(ii)), triggered by a broad CoC definition that expressly captures indirect ownership changes and reverse-triangular merger structures (Section 1.1(c)(iv)), reinforced by operation-of-law anti-assignment language routed through the same sole-discretion consent standard (Section 12.2). The $4M minimum annual commitment represents confirmed baseline exposure, with actual exposure potentially higher given Exhibit C tiering, and the embedded-systems dependency makes rapid resourcing difficult. The exposure falls below the $25M critical threshold, which prevents escalation to Critical, but the combination of absolute consent discretion, zero cure period, and infrastructure criticality warrants a High rating.

### hq-lease-crescent-ridge

This section addresses the Commercial Lease Agreement (Lease No. CRR-2018-4200-600), governing law Ohio, between Tenant Apex Industrial Technologies, Inc. and Landlord Crescent Ridge Realty Partners, LP, covering approximately 36,000 rentable square feet on the sixth floor of Crescent Ridge Tower, Cincinnati, Ohio, with an initial Term running July 1, 2018 through June 30, 2028.

**Change-of-Control Definition and Deemed Assignment (Sections 22.2 and 22.1)**

Section 22.2 provides one of the broadest change-of-control definitions reviewed in this deal. It defines three independent categories of "Deemed Assignment," each requiring Landlord's prior written consent: (a) "[a]ny change in control of Tenant, including without limitation any merger, consolidation, or transfer of a controlling interest in Tenant's equity, whether in a single transaction or a series of related transactions"; (b) any equity transfer "that results in a change in the identity of the person or group of persons that controls Tenant"; and (c) "[a]ny sale of all or substantially all of Tenant's assets." The definition of "control" is functional, capturing indirect influence "whether through the ownership of voting securities, by contract, or otherwise."

Critically, Section 22.2 closes every structural escape route: "The provisions of this Section 22.2 shall apply regardless of the form of the transaction, including without limitation any transaction structured as a forward or reverse merger, triangular merger, share exchange, asset acquisition, recapitalization, or similar combination." This explicit enumeration means the contemplated reverse-triangular merger structure triggers Section 22.2 on its face, with no ambiguity. Section 22.1 reinforces this independently by defining "assignment" to include "any assignment, transfer, or conveyance, whether voluntary or involuntary, by operation of law or otherwise" — the classic operation-of-law formulation that Ohio courts have recognized as capturing reverse mergers even where the target entity survives.

Section 22.2 also expressly states: "this Section 22 does not contain any exception or carve-out for Transfers or Deemed Assignments to or involving Affiliates of Tenant. Any Transfer or Deemed Assignment involving an Affiliate shall require Landlord's prior written consent in the same manner as any other Transfer." There is no Affiliate safe harbor whatsoever.

**Consent Standard and Conditions for Withholding (Section 22.3)**

Landlord's consent standard is reasonableness: "Landlord's consent to any Transfer or Deemed Assignment shall not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed." However, Section 22.3 enumerates five conditions under which withholding is per se reasonable, each of which must be evaluated against the Acquirer: (i) the proposed transferee's tangible net worth is less than the greater of Tenant's net worth as of the lease date or as of the transfer date — deal counsel must confirm the Acquirer satisfies this threshold; (ii) the proposed use is inconsistent with the Permitted Use; (iii) the transferee is a governmental entity; (iv) the Transfer would violate any other Lease provision or applicable law; and (v) an uncured Event of Default exists at the time of the Transfer. Failure on any single condition gives Landlord reasonable grounds to deny consent. Notably, Section 22.3 also contains a deemed-denial trap: "If Landlord fails to respond within such twenty (20) business day period, Landlord shall be deemed to have withheld its consent" — silence is a denial, not approval, placing the affirmative burden squarely on Tenant.

**Financial Consequence Chain (Sections 22.4(a) and 22.4(b))**

If Landlord withholds consent or Tenant effects an unauthorized Deemed Assignment, the financial consequence chain is as follows: Section 22.4(a) gives Landlord a hard termination right on "not less than one hundred twenty (120) days' prior written notice" with no cure period whatsoever — Section 12.1(d) confirms an unauthorized Deemed Assignment is itself an Event of Default, triggering Section 12.2's full remedies concurrently. Upon the Early Termination Date, Section 22.4(b) requires Tenant to pay "within thirty (30) days after the Early Termination Date, an early termination fee . . . in an amount equal to eighteen (18) months of the monthly Base Rent set forth in Section 1 of this Lease" — confirmed at $180,000.00 × 18 = **$3,240,000.00**. In addition, Section 12.2(c) permits Landlord to accelerate all remaining Rent through the Expiration Date discounted at 4% per annum; with annual Base Rent of $2,160,000.00 and approximately four years remaining at closing, accelerated Rent exposure could exceed $8 million before discounting, representing a compounded liability. The $360,000.00 Security Deposit held under Section 5 is expressly applicable toward the Early Termination Fee. The $2,160,000.00 annual Base Rent figure represents the annual contractual payment obligation; revenue concentration percentage was not extracted from available materials.

**Renewal Option (Section 3.3)**

Section 3.3 provides a five-year Renewal Option (July 1, 2028 – June 30, 2033) but expressly states it "is personal to Apex Industrial Technologies, Inc. and may not be exercised by or on behalf of any assignee, sublessee, or transferee without Landlord's prior written consent, which may be withheld in Landlord's sole discretion." This is a sole-discretion carve-out, not a reasonableness standard, meaning the Renewal Option's survival post-closing depends entirely on Landlord's goodwill and must be addressed in the consent negotiation.

Three instruments are cross-referenced: the Work Letter / Tenant Improvement Agreement (Exhibit C), reflecting a $1,440,000.00 TI Allowance for improvements that are now Landlord's property; the broker commission agreement with Meridian Commercial Realty Group, LLC (Section 25); and the SNDA referenced in Section 13, which should be reviewed to confirm non-disturbance protections are not conditioned on consent compliance.
